title: Understanding HOA Fees Before You Buy in a Planned Community
content_html:
Why HOA Fees Matter So Much in Temecula, Murrieta, and Menifee

Many of the planned communities across Temecula Valley, Murrieta, and Menifee are governed by a homeowners association, or HOA. These associations maintain shared amenities, enforce community standards, and collect regular fees (often called dues or assessments) from every homeowner to fund that work. If you're shopping for a home in a planned community, understanding how these fees work — and what they actually pay for — is just as important as comparing square footage or lot size.

Unlike a mortgage payment, an HOA fee isn't a fixed cost you lock in for the life of the loan. It can change over time, and it comes with rules, rights, and obligations that are worth understanding before you write an offer.

What HOA Fees Typically Cover

HOA dues vary widely depending on the community and the amenities it offers. Generally, these fees are used to fund things like:

  • Maintenance of common areas — landscaping, entry monuments, shared walkways
  • Amenities such as pools, clubhouses, parks, or sport courts
  • Reserve funds set aside for future large repairs (like roof replacement on shared structures or repaving private roads)
  • Insurance policies covering common areas
  • Management company fees for administering the association
  • In some communities, perimeter walls, gated entries, or private street maintenance

Some associations also cover services like trash pickup or basic landscaping for individual lots, which can make a fee look higher at first glance but actually replace costs you'd otherwise pay separately. This is why comparing two homes purely by their HOA fee amount, without understanding what's included, can be misleading.

Fees Can Change — Here's Why

California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act governs how homeowners associations are formed and operated, including the process by which an association's board may increase regular assessments or levy a special assessment — an additional charge, often one-time, to cover an unexpected or large expense such as a major repair not fully funded by reserves.[1] The specific rules governing how and when an association can raise dues or levy special assessments are also set out in that association's own governing documents (the CC&Rs, bylaws, and any rules adopted by the board), so it's worth reading those documents rather than assuming every association operates the same way.

Because HOA finances are managed by a volunteer board and a management company rather than a government entity, the health of the reserve fund can vary significantly from one community to the next. A well-funded reserve reduces the likelihood of a surprise special assessment; an underfunded one increases it.

Documents Buyers Should Review

When you're in escrow on a home within an HOA, you'll typically receive a package of association disclosure documents. These commonly include:

  • CC&Rs (Covenants, Conditions & Restrictions) — the core rules governing what you can and can't do with your property
  • Bylaws — how the association itself is governed and how the board is elected
  • Current budget and reserve study — a snapshot of the association's finances and how well future repairs are funded
  • Meeting minutes — recent board discussions, which can reveal upcoming projects, disputes, or planned assessments
  • Statement of assessments — confirms the current fee amount and whether the account is paid current

Reading through these documents — or having your agent and, where appropriate, a real estate attorney review them with you — is one of the most useful things you can do during your contingency period. It's much easier to negotiate or walk away before close of escrow than to discover an issue afterward.

Questions Worth Asking Before You Buy

  • What is the current monthly or annual HOA fee, and has it increased in recent years?
  • Are there any planned or discussed special assessments?
  • How much does the association hold in reserves, and how does that compare to its reserve study recommendations?
  • Are there restrictions that matter to your lifestyle — rental limits, RV or boat parking, exterior paint colors, pet restrictions?
  • What amenities are included, and are they well maintained?
  • Is the community age-restricted or does it have other occupancy rules?

Your agent can help you request and review this information as part of your purchase process, and can flag anything that looks like it needs a closer look before your contingency periods expire.

HOA Fees and Your Overall Budget

When you're calculating what you can afford, it's worth treating HOA dues as part of your monthly housing cost — similar to property taxes and insurance — rather than a minor add-on. Lenders generally factor recurring housing costs, which can include HOA dues, into the calculations used to qualify you for a mortgage, so it's worth asking your lender how a given community's fee would affect your specific loan approval amount.

It's also worth remembering that property tax bills in California can include more than just the base tax rate. Certain new communities are financed through Mello-Roos Community Facilities Districts, which allow local agencies to levy special taxes on properties within the district to fund infrastructure and services, and these charges appear as separate line items on the property tax bill.[2] These are distinct from HOA dues but are worth understanding together, since both affect your true monthly cost of ownership. Your agent or a tax professional can help you understand the specific line items on a property tax bill you're reviewing, and the Riverside County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder's office can provide records for a specific parcel.[3]

Weighing the Trade-Offs

An HOA isn't inherently a downside — for many buyers, the shared maintenance, amenities, and community standards are exactly what makes a planned community appealing. Consistent landscaping, well-kept common areas, and amenities like pools or parks can be worth the monthly cost. The key is going in with clear eyes: understanding what you're paying for, how that fee could change, and whether the community's rules fit how you actually want to live.

Taking the time to review HOA documents carefully during escrow — rather than skimming them — puts you in a much stronger position to make a confident decision about a home in a planned community.

Working With a Local Agent

Navigating HOA disclosures alongside inspections, financing, and negotiations can feel like a lot to track during a home purchase. George Khazanovskiy, a Temecula Valley real estate agent, can help you understand what to look for in HOA documents and how they fit into your overall home search across Temecula, Murrieta, and Menifee.
